notes: Schedule 21 murder minimum term appeal; unlawful knife possession as aggravating factor upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Richardson: Schedule 21 minimum term and unlawful knife possession
key_facts: The appellant pleaded guilty on re-arraignment to murder after stabbing a 55-year-old man in the neck during a dispute over stolen goods.
HHJ Milford QC fixed a 15-year starting point under Schedule 21 and a 14 years six months minimum term after six months' pre-sentence custody credit.
The judge treated the deceased as particularly vulnerable, unlawful public possession of a knife, prior affray and aggressive solicitation as aggravating factors balanced against mitigation.
The appellant argued unlawful knife possession was double-counted and that paragraph 10(b) vulnerability wording did not apply.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against minimum term imposed following guilty plea to murder in the Crown Court at Newcastle.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge was entitled to treat unlawful possession of a knife in a public place as an aggravating factor and the overall balance was not wrong.
enrichment.ratio: Under Schedule 21 unlawful possession of a knife in a public place may be an aggravating factor distinct from the use of the weapon in the fatal attack; deterrence applies where death ensues from unlawfully carried knives, following R v Peters and Attorney General's Reference No 33 of 1996.
legal_issues: Whether unlawful knife possession was double-counted in fixing the starting point
Whether a healthy 55-year-old man was particularly vulnerable under paragraph 10(b) of Schedule 21
Whether prior affray and aggressive solicitation were proper aggravating factors
Application of the two-stage Schedule 21 sentencing structure
linked_authorities: Attorney General's Reference No 33 of 1996 [1997] Cr App R(S) 10

confidence.notes: Sentencing reasoning and dismissal are clearly recorded; factual basis of plea limits some issues.

notes: Cannabis cultivation appeal after Class C reclassification; personal-use tariff reduced.

enrichment.short_title: Herridge: cannabis cultivation sentence after Class C reclassification
key_facts: The appellant pleaded guilty to cultivating 52 cannabis plants with ventilation and heating equipment at his rented premises.
The crop was consistent with personal use for a heavy habitual user who had attended drug services and pleaded at the earliest opportunity.
Judge Ball QC imposed 12 months imprisonment at Chelmsford Crown Court; counsel argued reclassification to Class C should reduce the tariff for personal-use cultivation.
The court reserved judgment because the case raised whether Parliament's reclassification should affect cultivation sentences where supply was not intended.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave of the single judge against sentence for cultivating cannabis contrary to section 6 of the 1971 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the 12-month sentence was quashed and substituted with six months imprisonment.
enrichment.ratio: Following cannabis reclassification, where section 6 cultivation is clearly for personal use alone a modest reduction in sentence reflects Parliament's less serious treatment of simple possession; Donovan and Mitchell exclude reductions where supply is involved, but personal-use cultivation remains custodial.
legal_issues: Whether Class C reclassification should reduce sentences for personal-use cannabis cultivation
Distinction between cultivation for supply and cultivation for personal use under section 6
Effect of Schedule 28 increased penalties for Class C supply offences
Appropriate tariff following Davy, Bennett and Evans

confidence.notes: Outcome and policy reasoning on reclassification are explicit though reserved-judgment context is noted.

notes: Fraud restitution amendment application; Peter Smith J grants amended money-had-and-received claim.

enrichment.short_title: OEM v Schneider: permission to amend restitution claim for director's fraud
key_facts: OEM plc alleged its late finance director Mr Schneider stole over £5 million by drawing cheques under £20,000 and falsifying books over seven years.
Some £2.35 million was paid into joint accounts with Mrs Schneider and £474,270 to Miss Schoeffler-Lubbock; probate was blocked by a caveat.
The claimant sought to amend to pursue money had and received and tracing into life policies and property without alleging knowing receipt.
Mrs Schneider argued receipt into a joint account was notional and Transvaal supported a conduit-pipe defence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory hearing on permission to amend particulars of claim and adjournment of defendants' Part 18 information applications.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to amend granted; defendants' information applications adjourned for schedules identifying alleged inadequacies; mediation encouraged for the third defendant.
enrichment.ratio: Credits to a husband-and-wife joint account from stolen company funds may prima facie support a money-had-and-received claim under Lipkin Gorman; whether restitution is unjust turns on trial facts including siphoning, change of position and use of funds, not on pre-amendment forensic demands.
legal_issues: Whether money credited to a joint account makes the innocent spouse liable for all stolen sums
Application of Transvaal v Atkinson conduit-pipe principles
Whether amendment should be refused for offshore company and Mr Noonan allegations
Scope of tracing at common law without constructive trust claims
linked_authorities: Transvaal & Delagoa Bay Investment Co Ltd v Atkinson [1944] 1 All ER 579

confidence.notes: Interlocutory ruling is detailed though final liability remains for trial.

notes: Staged crash fraud trial; police insurance funding and disclosure abuse-of-process grounds rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Hounsham: insurance-funded police investigation in staged crash fraud trial
key_facts: Three appellants were convicted of conspiracies to defraud insurers through staged road traffic accidents involving clocked prestige cars and stooge drivers.
During trial it emerged that Royal Sun Alliance, Direct Line and Norwich Union paid £4,500 towards Hampshire Police arrest-stage costs; PS Wade solicited contributions in 2002.
Defence applications to stay for abuse of process and to discharge the jury after inadvertent disclosure of Mayes's minor convictions were refused.
The prosecution conceded police acceptance of insurer payments was ultra vires but argued the conduct did not warrant staying proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave against convictions and refusals to stay proceedings or discharge the jury at Portsmouth Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; ultra vires insurer funding and late disclosure did not individually or cumulatively justify a stay, and the jury discharge application was rightly refused.
enrichment.ratio: Soliciting investigation funding from potential fraud victims is ultra vires and fraught with danger to police impartiality, but good-faith modest payments without demonstrated prejudice fall short of Bennett or Mullen exceptional abuse; non-deliberate disclosure failures that came to light at trial likewise do not require a stay.
legal_issues: Whether insurer payments to police vitiated the prosecution as an abuse of process
Whether funding documents should have been disclosed and their late discovery warranted a stay
Whether PS Wade acted in good faith in soliciting contributions
Whether inadvertent jury disclosure of minor convictions required discharge
linked_authorities: R v Horseferry Road Magistrates' Court, ex parte Bennett [1994] 1 AC 42

confidence.notes: Abuse-of-process principles and appellate disposition on each ground are comprehensively reasoned.

notes: Paroxetine patent cross-undertaking inquiry; preliminary issues refused, strike-out hearing ordered.

enrichment.short_title: SKB v Apotex: cross-undertaking inquiry and Canadian parties' standing
key_facts: SKB obtained interlocutory injunctions restraining Apotex from selling paroxetine hydrochloride anhydrate; the patent was ultimately held non-infringed though not revoked on appeal.
Cross-undertakings in damages became enforceable and Apotex Canada entities sought to recover manufacturers' and tabletting profits despite not being named defendants.
Pumfrey J faced applications to join Apotex Inc and Apotex Pharmachem, for preliminary issues on entitlement, and to strike out their claims.
Pleadings remained incomplete years after the Court of Appeal judgment because a 2003 order suspended timetables pending joinder.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Case management in an inquiry on cross-undertakings following successful non-infringement defence to patent proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Preliminary issue application refused; triability of Canadian parties' claims to be determined at a three-day hearing under CPR 3.4 and CPR 24; costs reserved.
enrichment.ratio: Novel fact-sensitive questions whether non-party group companies may enforce cross-undertakings by rectification, estoppel or third-party loss should not be decided as preliminary issues of law; strike-out threshold must be resolved first before any later preliminary issue directions.
legal_issues: Whether Apotex Inc and Apotex Pharmachem may recover on SKB's cross-undertaking
Whether preliminary issues should determine standing before full inquiry
Application of McLoughlin v Jones warnings on casual preliminary issue orders
Distinction between strike-out under CPR 3.4/24 and preliminary issue procedure

confidence.notes: Procedural directions are clear; substantive entitlement of Canadian parties remains undecided.

notes: Permission to appeal on King Fahd sovereign immunity; representation challenge refused.

enrichment.short_title: Harb v King Fahd: permission on sovereign immunity and marital claims
key_facts: Mrs Harb pursued claims against King Fahd Bin Abdul Aziz relating to their alleged marriage and financial arrangements.
She challenged the legitimacy of the King's representation through the Saudi embassy to English solicitors; the President dismissed the challenge as specious.
The President upheld sovereign immunity on 15 December 2004 applying a broad conventional appreciation of immunity bounds.
Counsel argued Fox on State Immunity suggests movement to restrict immunity in a ruler's private and domestic life and that Article 8 ECHR engagement is novel.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications for permission to appeal two interlocutory rulings of the President of the Family Division.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused on the representation challenge; permission granted on sovereign immunity for full court argument despite doubtful prospects.
enrichment.ratio: A late speculative challenge to a foreign sovereign's litigation authority without evidence may be dismissed summarily; nevertheless novel questions on whether absolute sovereign immunity extends to private marital claims engaging Article 8 justify permission to appeal for full argument.
legal_issues: Validity of the King's capacity and representation before the English court
Scope of sovereign immunity under the 1978 Act for private domestic claims
Interaction of state immunity with Article 8 ECHR family life
Whether Fox supports restricting immunity for rulers' private lives

confidence.notes: Short permission judgment; immunity appeal granted but merits not decided.

notes: GMC interim conditions extension for neurosurgeon; without-notice order with liberty to apply.

enrichment.short_title: GMC v Syed: extension of interim practice conditions for neurosurgeon
key_facts: Dr Syed faced interim conditions on his registration for about five years following assessors' findings of serious deficiencies in neurological surgery after incidents around 2000.
A performance assessment concluded deficiencies could be remedied by training but practice should remain limited; case examiners were considering fitness to practise.
The Interim Orders Panel found impaired fitness and risk to patients but imposed conditions as proportionate; existing conditions would expire on 28 May 2005.
Mr Syed was not notified of the hearing date and may have been in Pakistan; the GMC sought a one-year extension.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Without-notice High Court application to extend interim order of conditions pending fitness-to-practise proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Extension granted until 27 May 2006 with liberty for Dr Syed to apply on one week's notice to vary or discharge the order.
enrichment.ratio: Where interim GMC conditions are supported by cogent performance-assessment evidence and imminent expiry creates urgency, the court may extend without notice but should protect the doctor's position by granting liberty to apply promptly if he wishes to contest continuation.
legal_issues: Whether interim conditions should be extended for a further year
Procedural fairness where the doctor was not notified of the hearing
Whether performance assessment evidence justified continued restrictions
Balancing public protection against consequences for the practitioner

confidence.notes: Short ex tempore judgment with clear order and protective liberty-to-apply term.

notes: Interim care orders for siblings with complex medical needs; Article 8 ultra vires point rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Westminster v RA: interim care orders and multi-agency fairness challenge
key_facts: Westminster sought interim care orders for siblings B (5) and S (3 months) with Seckel Syndrome, cataracts, feeding difficulties and complex medical needs.
The mother had a history of secret marriage, domestic abuse, B's unregistered birth and delayed reporting of B's disappearance before her reappearance severely unwell.
The Council planned community-based parenting assessment with shared parental responsibility rather than foster care; the mother initially agreed then objected via counsel.
Counsel argued failure to hold a pre-proceedings multi-disciplinary case conference rendered the application ultra vires and breached Article 8.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court hearing on interim care order applications transferred from the family proceedings court on an alleged ultra vires/fairness point.
enrichment.outcome: Interim care orders granted approving community-based interim care plans; the ultra vires and Article 8 procedural challenge was rejected as unmeritorious.
enrichment.ratio: Article 8 requires transparent parental involvement throughout child protection decision-making, but a conference held shortly after issue without objection and prior parental agreement does not invalidate interim care proceedings; threshold criteria were met given acute medical needs and uncertainty over parental support.
legal_issues: Whether failure to hold a pre-proceedings case conference breached Article 8
Whether the Council acted ultra vires in issuing care proceedings
Whether section 31 threshold criteria were satisfied
Appropriateness of community versus residential parenting assessment
linked_authorities: Re G (Care: Challenge to local authority's decision) [2003] EWHC 551 (Fam)
Re L (Care: Assessment: Fair Trial) [2002] EWHC 1379 (Fam)

confidence.notes: Detailed chronology and clear rejection of the procedural human-rights challenge.

notes: VAT sports exemption appeal; Kennemer applied to reject group subsidiary structure.

enrichment.short_title: Messenger Leisure v HMRC: VAT exemption for proprietary golf club supplies
key_facts: Developments Ltd supplied sporting facilities at Messenger group proprietary golf clubs using Leisure's courses rent-free to claim VAT exemption as a non-profit making body.
The company accumulated large surpluses, was wholly owned by Leisure, and was set up after Kennemer to obtain fiscal advantage though Mr Shah said he sought affordable family sporting facilities.
The tribunal found de facto profit distribution via interest-free loans to Leisure and capital improvements benefiting Leisure's land; Hart J upheld rejection of exemption.
The Court of Appeal held Kennemer does not make non-distribution sufficient; Developments' aim was commercially to further the Messenger group.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from dismissal of VAT tribunal decision rejecting exemption for supplies from September 1998 to February 2001.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Developments was not a non-profit-making organisation under Article 13A(1)(m) and its supplies were taxable.
enrichment.ratio: Kennemer holds only that systematic surpluses need not disqualify a genuinely non-profit-making body if profits are not distributed; an integral commercial group subsidiary whose aim is to further the parent's proprietary business and accumulate reserves conferring financial advantage on members is not exempt even if its memorandum restricts distributions.
legal_issues: Meaning of non-profit-making organisation under Article 13A(1)(m) after Kennemer
Whether fiscal-advantage corporate structuring precludes VAT sports exemption
Subjective intentions of controller versus objective commercial aim
Effect of parent company's power to alter constitution and access surpluses
linked_authorities: Kennemer Golf and Country Club v Staatssecretaris van Financien (C-174/00)
Customs and Excise Commissioners v Zoological Society of London (C-267/00)
Gregg v Commissioners of Customs & Excise (C-216/97)

confidence.notes: Full three-judge appellate judgment with detailed Kennemer analysis and clear result.

notes: Health and Safety railway derailment fine appeal; public-service deterrence but fine reduced.

enrichment.short_title: Jarvis Facilities: health and safety fine for railway junction derailment

statutes_considered.title: Health and Safety at Work Act 1974

key_facts: Jarvis Facilities Ltd pleaded guilty after a freight train derailed at Aldwarke junction when diverted onto track where rail had been removed following unrecorded plainlining work.
Plainlining closed Roundwood Chord access but clipping, scotching and signaller book entries were not properly completed; an unrelated works error removed the signal sleeve.
No significant injury occurred; collision risk was limited because red signals protected the line and junction speed was 25mph.
The company was fined £400,000 at Sheffield Crown Court; a sister company had earlier been fined £500,000 at York for graver railway safety failures.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave of the full court against sentence for breach of section 3(1) of the 1974 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; fine reduced from £400,000 to £275,000 with costs unchanged.
enrichment.ratio: Health and safety fines must reflect gravity of breach, deterrence and company means; public-service railway failures entrusted with public safety may attract greater severity than comparable private-sector breaches, but the judge here overstated the actual risk generated on these particular facts.
legal_issues: Appropriate fine level following R v F Howe & Sons guidance
Whether public-service context justifies higher penalties
Assessment of actual versus potential risk from signalling and track removal failures
Effect of related Jarvis Fastline York proceedings as aggravating context
linked_authorities: R v F Howe & Sons (Engineers) Ltd [1999] 2 Cr App Rep (S) 37
